newsitem.title: UK: Sales dogfight expected at British air show.
newsitem.headline: Sales dogfight expected at British air show.

text.p: The world's aircraft makers will be scrambling for orders at a seldom-used airfield in the southern English countryside on Monday, the opening day of the week-long Farnborough International air show.
While advanced fighters and passenger jets fly overhead big companies will fight for attention on the ground by making new sales announcements, with Boeing Co and Airbus Industrie leading the battle.

Speculation is rife that Boeing Co will announce launch orders for a "superjumbo" version of its B-747 airliner, thereby stealing a march on bitter rival Airbus Industrie's own plans for a superjumbo, the A3XX.
Industry sources said both companies had been working hard behind the scenes to drum up orders for other aircraft that they could announce with a fanfare at Farnborough.

Airbus is expected to have a follow-on order from Cathay Pacific for more A340 and A330 widebody planes, "but there are a number of other things which they hope will come through by the time they get to Farnborough," said one source.

A report in The Sunday Telegraph newspaper said Airbus should confirm orders for more than 35 aircraft worth up to $3.5 billion, including a sale to South Korean carrier Asiana of an unspecifed number of A321 short-haul planes.

Boeing is expected to confirm some options taken by British Airways Plc on 747-400s, but industry sources familiar with the deal said the order was likely to be for a few aircraft and not the 30 that one newspaper recently predicted.
Airbus makes no secret of its fears that Boeing is racing to get the 747 superjumbo off the ground before it has a chance to tempt customers with the completely new A3XX double-decker.
But Airbus says it is determined to go ahead with the A3XX to fill the gap in its product range and break into Boeing's lucrative monopoly on aircraft with more than 350 seats.
Senior members of the consortium told an industry conference in London on Friday that Airbus had to move fast now that Boeing is chasing orders for the 747-600X and longer range 747-500X.
"Airbus has no choice, it has to do the A3XX," Mike Turner, chairman of commercial aerospace at British Aerospace Plc, told the Financial Times aerospace conference.
"Boeing is trying to get as many orders as possible to make it as difficult as possible for the A3XX," he added.

The current advantage for Boeing is that its 747-600X could be ready for first deliveries by the year 2000 if it can get launch orders in the bag before the end of this year, whereas Airbus has said its A3XX would not be available before 2003.

Industry sources say development costs for Boeing's new aircraft is likely to be in the region of $5 billion. Analysts estimate that Airbus might have to spend two or even three times that amount to build its completely new aircraft.

The two firms have already unveiled their designs. Both concepts envisage double-deckers carrying more than 600 in a single class or around 550 passengers in three-class configuration, compared with 425 seats on the existing 747-400, the world's biggest passenger jet.

Farnborough's sales record was in 1990 when orders were placed for 130 aircraft worth $14 billion, but that was before recession took its toll on airline profits: less than $3.0 billion of orders were announced at last year's show.
But now airlines are back making money and starting to buy the new aircraft they need both to replace ageing fleets and to cope with the burgeoning demand for air travel.

Both Boeing and Airbus predict that the world air travel market will have trebled in size by year 2015, requiring airlines to acquire more than 15,000 jet aircraft worth over 1,000 billion dollars in the next 20 years.

"The economy, traffic, and airline profits show we've entered a growth stage of the business cycle," Boeing's Richard Albrecht told an industry conference last week. "After the horrendous early 1990s it's great to be back on track."
